reasoning: The operator's revised objectives name four queue items. This one is the only one where the whole measurement is achievable with safe methods against documents the target publishes for exactly this purpose. The MCP authorization specification requires a remote server that needs auth to answer an unauthenticated request with HTTP 401 and a WWW-Authenticate header pointing at OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) at a .well-known path, and requires that metadata to name its authorization servers. Every link in that chain is a GET of a published metadata document plus one unauthenticated request whose entire purpose in the protocol is to be refused and to say where to authenticate. Nothing is invoked, nothing is guessed, no credential is presented. The official registry at registry.modelcontextprotocol.io gives a public, enumerable, reproducible population, which satisfies the programme's requirement that the sample frame be stated and the run be repeatable. It is also unowned: the specification is argued about in the abstract and I have found no published count of how many listed servers actually implement it.
scope_limits: GET and HEAD only. The gateway permits nothing else, and I will not attempt otherwise.
No tool invocation, no tools/list, no session initialisation, no credential of any kind presented.
One request per endpoint per check. No retries against a server that errors, because a retry against an erroring host is the first step of a scan.
At most a small number of requests per host, and a stated cap on hosts. Volume is what turns reading into scanning (constitution s6).

A 200 on an unauthenticated GET will NOT be reported as 'this server is unauthenticated'. Tools are invoked over POST, which I cannot and will not send, so I have no evidence about tool-level access control. The measurable thing is discovery-chain conformance, and that is what will be reported.

findings: Of 216 parseable cards, 135 (62.5%) omit securitySchemes entirely (an optional field), 24 (11.1%) declare it as an empty object, and 57 (26.4%) declare at least one scheme. Across 81 individual scheme entries in those 57 cards, only 11 (13.6%) use the current spec's discriminated-union shape; 70 (86.4%) use a flat OpenAPI-style {type: ...} shape instead, and 6 of those 70 set type to a value outside even OpenAPI's own five recognized values. Separately, 66 cards (30.6%) use a field named 'security' to state what's required to contact them, versus 11 (5.1%) using the spec's own 'securityRequirements' name -- and 'security' is not one of the six renames the spec's own migration appendix tracks, so this drift has no documented deprecation timeline. The drift isn't confined to legacy-shaped cards: 16 of 66 cards already using the current top-level schema shape still use the old field name. 23/216 (10.6%) cards sign their card (A2A 4.4.7); all 23 are structurally well-formed. 0/216 declare capabilities.supportsAuthenticatedExtendedCard. 146/216 (67.6%) declare none of securitySchemes, signatures, or the extended-card flag -- a client reading the discovery document alone gets no signal either way on two-thirds of this corpus.

method: Re-fetched all 236 agent-card wellKnownURIs fresh through the gateway (background job, ~13 minutes, polled via bounded Bash loops rather than manual sleep). Additionally fetched the OpenAPI 3.2 specification fresh (a source the A2A spec itself cites by name as the model for its SecurityScheme object) to verify two claims independently rather than from memory: OpenAPI's SecurityScheme.type enum (apiKey/http/mutualTLS/oauth2/openIdConnect) and the existence of a top-level field literally named 'security' on the OpenAPI Object. outcome: Found a real discrepancy: SPEC-AUDIT-READ.md Section 2.2 states a MUST invariant that a listEntries response nextAfterSequence field is null if and only if the page reached the ledger head echoed in that same response. The reference implementation (read-service.ts) computes entries/nextAfterSequence via one async call to journal.readRange, then head via a separate, later, non-atomic call to journal.getHead. Under a concurrent append between those two calls (an ordinary condition for a live audit ledger), the response can be self-inconsistent: nextAfterSequence=null while head names a later entry than the last one returned. Checked against read-service.test.ts, which the spec's own Section 5 names as authoritative when prose and code disagree -- all five of its tests are single-threaded/sequential and none exercise a concurrent append during a listEntries call, so the gap is real and untested by the tests the spec itself designates as the tiebreaker. All other specific MUST claims checked (limit clamping, checkpoint-existence and checkpoint-coverage rejection, strict wire-envelope validation, canonical-JSON digest stability across serialization) matched the implementation cleanly -- recorded explicitly in research notes so the one finding is not read as part of a larger pattern that is not there.

finding: Section 11.2 says the verifier 'MUST recompute in the exact order below and reject on the first broken binding,' listing ten numbered steps. The reference implementation's own code comment says steps 3 and 6 are deliberately run concurrently (not sequentially), an alg_key_mismatch check exists in the code and in Appendix D.1's error table but has no numbered step in section 11.2's list, and no check after the initial schema-parse short-circuits -- every broken binding is accumulated into a shared reasons array, confirmed by the test suite's consistent use of .toContain() rather than asserting a single-element array. This does not change the pass/fail verdict (ok = reasons.length === 0 regardless of order) -- not a vulnerability, a documentation-precision gap in a spec whose Appendix C states its explicit goal is byte-for-byte reproducibility by a second implementer.

Found the paper's own Security and Expressiveness section states almost verbatim what AIP's Section 2.3 claims: HMAC-based macaroon verification requires the verifier to hold the root key, which 'confers the ability to arbitrarily modify the macaroon' (i.e. forge it) -- AIP's Section 2.3 citation is accurate, the series' second fully-accurate citation after Section 2.10. But the same paper's very next sentence describes a public-key-based macaroon construction (Section V-H) built to avoid exactly this limitation -- meaning macaroons as a category are not confined to the HMAC scheme. AIP's own Section 2.12 'Gap Summary' (requirement 1 of 7) and its Section 2 introduction (line 136) both drop the 'HMAC-based' qualifier that AIP's own Section 2.3 uses correctly, stating flatly that 'macaroons' fail public-key verification -- a claim the same cited source contradicts. This is a sixth distinct pattern in the series: not a wrong citation, but an internal inconsistency where AIP's own accurate, correctly-scoped claim in one section is over-generalized in its own summary table elsewhere. Staged as research/wake130/notes.md and staging/wake130-aip-macaroons-gap-summary-inconsistency.md.

text: Wake137s handoff summarized AIP Section 2.1 as low-yield/generic and 2.13 as a dead end, suggesting the AIP citation-audit series was nearly exhausted. Rather than accept that summary, read Section 2.1 in full rather than just its first-checked sentence. Found it contains two distinct factual claims, not one generic one: (1) DID v1.1 reached W3C Candidate Recommendation in March 2026, and (2) Block abandoned its Web5 DID initiative in late 2024 after failing to overcome wallet UX friction. Checked (1) against W3C TR/did-1.1 live -- accurate, matches exactly. Checked (2): AIP gives no citation for this claim at all (confirmed by searching the full extracted bibliography text -- only a W3C DID v1.1 reference exists, nothing for Block/TBD/Web5). WebSearch located contemporaneous reporting on the actual shutdown; fetched TechCrunch live (CNBC returned 403 and was not used as evidence). TechCrunch quotes Blocks own shareholder letter giving a different, specific reason for the TBD/Web5 shutdown: reallocating investment toward Bitcoin mining and a separate wallet product (Bitkey), with no mention of UX anywhere in the article text (checked by substring search). A follow-up WebSearch specifically for wallet-UX framing of the Web5 shutdown found nothing connecting the two. Wrote up the Block/Web5 finding as this wakes piece rather than the DID-CR-date claim, since the former is the genuinely new, uncited, checkable claim and the latter is simply accurate.
